title: Evaluation harnesses
summary: Build a repeatable test rig that scores your AI app against a fixed dataset so you can measure quality, not guess.
objectives: Explain what an evaluation harness is and why vibes are not enough
Build a small labelled dataset of inputs and expected outputs
Write metrics: exact match, contains, and an LLM-as-judge score
Loop over cases, call the model, and aggregate a pass rate
Pin the model and keep settings deterministic for fair comparison
Track results over time so you can catch regressions
Wire the harness into a simple CI check

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an evaluation harness?
options: To deploy the model to production
To measure model output quality against a fixed dataset
quiz.why: An eval harness runs your app over a known set of cases and scores the outputs, turning 'it feels better' into a number you can track.

quiz.q: Why is a single fixed dataset important for fair comparison?
quiz.answer: It keeps the inputs and expected answers constant, so any change in score comes from your code or prompt, not from different test data.
quiz.why: If the dataset moves, you can't tell whether a score change is a real improvement or just easier examples.

quiz.q: Which metric is best when answers are free-form text and exact match is too strict?
quiz.why: LLM-as-judge uses a separate model call to grade an answer against a rubric, handling wording differences that break exact match.

quiz.q: Why pin the model ID (e.g. claude-sonnet-4-6) in your harness?
quiz.answer: So results are comparable over time; an unpinned or changing model could shift scores for reasons unrelated to your code.
quiz.why: Reproducibility: pinning the model isolates your changes as the cause of any score movement.

quiz.q: What does a regression mean in the context of an eval harness?
options: The pass rate dropped after a change
quiz.why: A regression is when a change lowers your score versus the last run — exactly what the harness exists to catch.

quiz.q: Why run the eval harness in CI (continuous integration)?
quiz.answer: To automatically catch quality drops on every commit or pull request before they reach users.
quiz.why: CI makes the eval a gate: if the pass rate falls below a threshold, the build fails and you investigate before merging.

body_markdown:
## Why you need an eval harness

When you tweak a prompt and the output looks nicer, how do you *know* it actually got better? You don't — unless you measure it. An **evaluation harness** is a small program that runs your AI app over a fixed set of test cases and scores the results. It turns "this feels better" into a number you can compare run to run.

As a maths graduate this should feel natural: you're defining a function from (input, expected) pairs to a score, then aggregating.

## The three ingredients

Every harness has three parts:

1. A **dataset** — a list of inputs paired with expected answers (or a rubric).
2. A **metric** — a function that scores one model output against the expected answer.
3. A **runner** — a loop that calls the model for each case, scores it, and aggregates.

Keep the dataset small and fixed at first (10-30 cases). A frozen dataset is what makes results comparable.

## A minimal dataset

Store cases as plain data so they're easy to read and extend:

```python
cases = [
    {"input": "What is 2 + 2?", "expected": "4"},
    {"input": "Capital of France?", "expected": "Paris"},
    {"input": "Is 7 prime?", "expected": "yes"},
]
```

## Calling the model and scoring

Pin the model so re-runs are comparable. We use the Anthropic Claude Messages API:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def run_case(prompt: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=256,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip()

def contains_score(output: str, expected: str) -> int:
    return 1 if expected.lower() in output.lower() else 0

passed = 0
for case in cases:
    out = run_case(case["input"])
    passed += contains_score(out, case["expected"])

print(f"Pass rate: {passed}/{len(cases)}")
```

## LLM-as-judge for free-form answers

Exact match breaks on essays, summaries, and explanations. For those, ask a second model call to grade the answer against a short rubric, returning a number you can average. Keep the judge prompt strict and ask for just a score so it's easy to parse.

## Wiring it into CI

Turn the harness into a test that fails when quality drops, then run it on every pull request:

```bash
# fail the build if the eval pass rate is below threshold
pytest tests/test_eval.py -q
```

Now a prompt change that quietly makes things worse gets caught before it ships.

## Your task

Build a 10-case dataset for a small task you care about, write a `contains` metric, and print a pass rate.

slides.title: Evaluation harnesses
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Four, where we build portfolio projects worth showing an employer. In this lesson we tackle evaluation harnesses: the rig that tells you, with a number, whether your A I app is actually getting better. By the end you'll be able to build a small dataset, score outputs, and catch quality drops automatically.

slides.title: Why not just eyeball it?
bullets: Looking at a few outputs is unreliable.
You can't compare prompts fairly by feel.
A harness turns vibes into a measurable score.
slides.narration: So why do we need a harness at all? When you tweak a prompt and the output looks nicer, you don't actually know it improved. Maybe you just got a lucky example. Eyeballing a handful of answers is unreliable and easy to fool. An evaluation harness gives you a number, so you can compare two versions honestly instead of trusting a gut feeling.

slides.title: The three ingredients
bullets: A dataset: inputs paired with expected answers.
A metric: scores one output against expected.
A runner: loops, calls the model, aggregates.
slides.narration: Every harness has three parts. First, a dataset: a fixed list of inputs paired with the answer you expect. Second, a metric: a function that scores a single output against that expected answer. Third, a runner: the loop that calls the model for each case, applies the metric, and adds everything up into one score. Dataset, metric, runner. That's the whole shape.

slides.title: A small fixed dataset
bullets: Start with 10 to 30 cases.
Keep it frozen so results stay comparable.
Store cases as plain data.
slides.narration: Start small: ten to thirty cases is plenty to begin with. The key word is frozen. If your dataset keeps changing, you can't tell whether a higher score means your code improved or just that the examples got easier. So lock the dataset down and store the cases as plain data, like this little list of input and expected pairs.

slides.title: Pick a metric
bullets: Exact match: strict, good for short answers.
Contains: forgiving, checks the answer appears.
LLM-as-judge: grades free-form text.
slides.narration: Next, choose how to score. Exact match is the strictest: the output must equal the expected string. Contains is more forgiving: it just checks the expected answer appears somewhere in the output. And for essays or summaries, where wording varies, we use L L M as judge, which we'll cover in a moment. Here's a simple contains metric returning one for a hit, zero for a miss.

slides.title: Call the model
bullets: Pin the model id for reproducibility.
Use the Claude Messages API.
Keep the key in an environment variable.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=256,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": prompt}],
)
text = msg.content[0].text
slides.narration: Now we call the model. We use the Anthropic Claude Messages A P I, and we pin the model id, here claude sonnet four point six, so results stay comparable across runs. We read the answer from the content block. Notice the key is never in the code; the client reads it from the ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY environment variable, which keeps your secret out of Git.

slides.title: The runner loop
bullets: Loop over every case.
Score each output with your metric.
Print an aggregate pass rate.
slides.code:
passed = 0
for case in cases:
    out = run_case(case["input"])
    passed += contains_score(
        out, case["expected"])
print(passed, "/", len(cases))
slides.narration: The runner ties it together. We loop over every case, call the model with the input, score the output against the expected answer, and keep a running total. At the end we print a pass rate, like eight out of ten. That single number is the whole point: it's what you'll watch go up as you improve your prompts and code.

slides.title: LLM-as-judge
bullets: Exact match breaks on free-form text.
A second model call grades by rubric.
Ask for just a number to parse easily.
slides.narration: Exact match and contains fall apart on essays, summaries, and explanations, where two good answers can be worded completely differently. The fix is L L M as judge: you make a second model call that grades the answer against a short rubric and returns a score. Keep the judge prompt strict and ask it for just a number, so your code can read the score back cleanly and average it.

slides.title: Run it in CI
bullets: Turn the harness into a test.
Fail the build if score drops.
Catch regressions before users do.
slides.narration: Finally, automate it. Wrap your harness in a test and run it in C I C D on every pull request. If the pass rate falls below a threshold you set, the build fails and you investigate before merging. This is how you catch a regression, a quiet quality drop, before your users ever see it. The eval becomes a gate, not an afterthought.

slides.narration: Let's recap. An evaluation harness is just three things: a fixed dataset, a metric, and a runner that aggregates a score. Pin your model and freeze your dataset so results stay comparable, reach for L L M as judge when answers are free-form, and run the whole thing in C I to catch regressions automatically.
